title: 8-week Forward Deployed Engineer plan
summary: Coding and SQL on messy data, customer discovery and case interviews, building and debugging in customer environments, then LLM apps or data integration and full mock loops. About 8–10 hours a week.

rhythm.text: Two coding or SQL problems, or one lesson and a guide: 25 minutes to solve, 10 to review, then rewrite one from memory.
Customer or system design reading and a one-page note: scope, load plan, runbook or pilot plan.
One 45-minute mock (coding, design or customer case) with a written debrief, then a story, a 15-minute weekly review and an error-log update.

rules: Talk out loud while you solve, as you would in the interview.
State the time and space complexity before you code.
Test edge cases: empty input, one item, duplicates, and the largest size.
Log every miss with why it happened and the fix.
In every design or case answer, restate the customer’s goal and how success will be measured before you propose a solution.

python: collections.Counter counts in one pass, and defaultdict(list) groups without checking for missing keys.
Use collections.deque for queues: popleft() is O(1), while list.pop(0) is O(n).
heapq is a min-heap on a plain list. Push (priority, item) tuples, and negate the priority for a max-heap.
bisect_left and bisect_right binary-search a sorted list for you.
sorted(items, key=lambda r: (r[1], -r[0])) sorts by several keys. list.sort() sorts in place and returns None.
Recursion stops at about 1,000 frames by default. Use an explicit stack for deep trees and graphs.
Integers never overflow, and float("inf") is a clean starting minimum.
Read messy input defensively: strip and lower-case text keys, and convert numbers inside try/except ValueError so one bad row does not stop the load.
typescript: Use Map and Set for lookups and counts: keys keep their type, and size and insertion order come built in.
There is no built-in heap. Write a small binary heap (an array with sift-up and sift-down) that takes a comparator.
There is no deque. For a BFS queue, keep an array and a head index; shift() can cost O(n).
sort() compares as strings by default: [10, 9, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 9]. Pass (a, b) => a - b for numbers.
Numbers are 64-bit floats, exact up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 − 1). Use BigInt beyond that, and Math.floor for integer division.
Type the signature first, e.g. function topK(nums: number[], k: number): number[], and narrow nullable nodes before using them.
Infinity and -Infinity are clean starting values for a minimum or maximum.
Parse untrusted input at the edge: Number("") is 0 and Number("abc") is NaN, so check for empty text and use Number.isFinite before trusting a value.

weeks.title: Hashing, windows and messy input
weeks.focus: Hash maps for counting, grouping and deduplication, sliding windows, and interval merges: the shapes that show up when you clean real customer data.

tip.python: Normalise keys once: key = email.strip().lower(). A dict from key to the best row so far deduplicates in one pass, and comparing (updated, id) tuples settles ties.
tip.typescript: Normalise keys once: email.trim().toLowerCase(). A Map from key to the best row so far deduplicates in one pass. Compare updated first, then id, since arrays do not compare element by element.

weeks.title: SQL for messy data, and graphs
weeks.focus: Joins, upserts and deduplication in SQL, plus graph traversal for merging records that share identifiers.

tip.python: For graphs, build adjacency with defaultdict(list) and use collections.deque for BFS. For union-find, keep a parent dict and compress paths as you find roots.
tip.typescript: For graphs, build adjacency as a Map<string, string[]>. For BFS, keep an array and a head index instead of shift(), which can cost O(n).

weeks.title: APIs, auth and safe retries
weeks.focus: How customer systems talk to yours: authentication, idempotent writes, webhooks, retries, and small stateful components such as rate limiters.

tip.python: Raise specific exceptions with context, e.g. raise ValueError(f"row {i}: bad email {email!r}"), and catch the narrowest type. Always pass a timeout to network calls.
tip.typescript: fetch only rejects on network errors, so check response.ok yourself. It has no default timeout: pass signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000).

tip.python: Prototype with plain functions and dataclasses, then add type hints at the boundaries. A few assert-style tests on the core function keep a fast demo from breaking live.
tip.typescript: Prototype with plain functions and type the boundaries first. Use unknown for parsed input and narrow it, rather than any, so bad data fails loudly.

tip.python: Use the logging module with one logger per module and structured fields, not print. Log the exception with logger.exception inside except so the traceback is kept.
tip.typescript: Wrap awaits at the boundary and log error.cause as well as the message. An unhandled rejection can end a Node process, so never leave a promise floating.

tip.python: Keep prompts as templates with named fields and build them in one function you can test. Use generators to stream chunks rather than loading every document at once.
tip.typescript: Keep prompts as typed template functions, e.g. (q: string, docs: Doc[]) => string. Stream with for await...of over an async iterator rather than buffering everything.

tip.python: Process large files with generators so memory stays flat: read a row, validate it, yield it. itertools.groupby needs input sorted by the same key.
tip.typescript: Process large inputs in batches and await each one, so memory and connections stay bounded. Validate every row before it reaches the database.
